name: Femi Khan

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello, and thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. What you tell me stays confidential, so you can say what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, what does a normal working day look like for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I buy phone chargers, cables, cases and speakers for Volt Trade, which sells to about four hundred small shops. My day starts with sales numbers from yesterday, then I decide what to reorder from the factories and trading companies overseas. A lot of it is judging what will be hot next month, like a new phone launch that makes every old case useless. I enjoy the guessing game, but the margins are tiny and it's a race to the bottom.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My partner Tolu runs a small hair salon with a friend, so her income goes up and down with the season. We have Zainab, twelve, and Idris, nine, and a mortgage we took when rates were lower. I'm 43, and I only became a buyer five years ago after working in the returns department, so I'm still junior and still learning how to read the market.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's fine, useful but overhyped. At work I'd say it helps with product descriptions and that's it. Online I'd post that AI is a good assistant and a bad boss.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, nothing changes much, but I'm still uneasy because of the business, not the tech. Volt Trade is squeezed by the big online marketplaces that sell cheaper, and the shops we supply are closing. If we lose another five shops, my hours or my job could be next, whatever AI does.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on and use AI for the dull stuff. I'd keep using it to check forecasts and write product listings. I'd also put more energy into my side business, buying and reselling refurbished phones online, to get another three hundred a month. And I'd pay extra on the mortgage when I can.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels like standing on a market stall that's slowly getting emptier. Not a panic, just a steady worry about the numbers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say is the weak spot in your firm?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The weak spot is that we compete on price against people who have more money than we do. We don't have our own brand. If the small shops stop buying, we've got nothing to hold on to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you resell on the side. How does that fit in?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I buy used phones from a guy who clears out corporate stock, clean them up and sell on a marketplace site. It makes about two hundred a month on a good one. It's a bit of insurance, and Tolu says it's a distraction, though she'd still prefer I have the extra.

say: I'd say it's **useful but overhyped**, a good assistant and a bad boss.
I'd tell colleagues it helps with product descriptions and little else.
think: Even without AI, **Volt Trade** is squeezed by cheaper online sellers and closing shops.
If we lose another five shops, my hours or job could go.
do: Use AI for forecasts and product listings, as I do now.
Grow my side business reselling **refurbished phones** to add three hundred a month.
Overpay the mortgage when I can.
feel: Like a **market stall** that's slowly emptying; steady worry, not panic.
S0.quote: The weak spot is that we compete on price against people who have more money than we do.
fieldNote: Threat is **business** margins and closing shops, which he names before AI comes up.
Already has a side business reselling phones, which shows his comfort with risk and tools.

steps.text: Use AI to check sales forecasts and write product listings
Resell refurbished phones online for an extra three hundred a month
Overpay the mortgage whenever the side business pays out

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's good, if you learn it early. At work I'd show the others the prompts I use. Online I'd say the winners will be the people who adapt, and the losers the ones who pretend it isn't happening.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I think reorder planning and price checks go to software, and that's maybe sixty percent of the buying job. Volt Trade will probably cut two or three buyers of the seven. I'm the least experienced, but I know the tools better than most of them, which might save me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd offer to build an AI forecasting workflow for the team, and put my name on it. I'd start a short online course in e-commerce analytics, and grow my side resale into a proper small shop on a marketplace. In the first year I'd aim for a title like category analyst, not just buyer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels like a race, and I'm one of the faster runners, but I still wonder if the track is going to disappear.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would be the first job you let the tools take?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Price checks, without doubt. The software can scan thousands of listings in a minute, and I can't. I'd happily give it up to focus on supplier calls, but they'd probably need one person for that, not seven.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would Tolu and you split the risk?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tolu's income depends on the salon, and hair doesn't go to software for a long time. If I lost my job we'd lean on hers and my side income. It'd be tight for a few months, but we have about four months saved, so it wouldn't be a disaster.

say: I'd say **learn it early**, and show others the prompts I use.
I'd say the winners adapt and the losers pretend it isn't happening.
think: Reorder planning and price checks, about **sixty percent**, go to software, and Volt Trade will cut two or three of seven buyers.
I know the tools better than most colleagues, which might save me.
do: Offer to build an AI **forecasting workflow** and put my name on it.
Start an online e-commerce analytics course.
Grow my resale side business into a proper marketplace shop.
feel: A **race** where I'm a fast runner but the track might disappear.
S1.quote: The winners will be the people who adapt, and the losers the ones who pretend it isn't happening.
fieldNote: Adaptive and quick, but still believes the track may **disappear** under him in a few years.
Says his partner Tolu's hands-on salon income is the lasting backstop for the household.

steps.text: Build an AI forecasting workflow for the Volt Trade buying team
Start an online e-commerce analytics course
Turn the phone resale side job into a proper marketplace shop

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got to move now, and I'd show anyone who'd listen what the tools can do. At work I'd say we should shift to selling our own brand and services, because buying alone is finished. Online I'd say stay calm and get your skills up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, this is the one where my job goes. If AI can do any thinking job better and cheaper, a buyer is just a person approving what the machine suggests. I'm junior and I'd be one of the first out, even though I'm good with tools.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd run at it. I'd turn my resale side business into something real, maybe a small online shop that sells refurbished phones, with proper stock and a few repeat customers. I'd save everything I could, aiming for six months of expenses. And I'd talk to the people at Volt Trade about moving into a hands-on role, like warehouse quality control.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels like a jolt, but I'm more thrilled than frozen. Underneath, I'm afraid of the mortgage, and that does wake me at night.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Imagine telling your boss this is coming in two years. What happens?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my boss, you either make us the company that uses this, or we don't exist in two years. Probably he'd say no, and then I'd start looking at start-ups that need people who already know the tools. I'd rather leave early than be last.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do with the money side first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First I'd cut the things we don't need, subscriptions and the car upgrade, and put every spare pound into savings. Then I'd talk to the bank about whether we can fix our mortgage rate. Tolu's salon income helps, and robots doing hair is a long way off.

say: I'd say **move now**, and show anyone who'd listen what the tools can do.
I'd say buying alone is finished, so we should sell our own brand.
think: This is the one where my job **goes**, because a buyer just approves what the machine suggests.
I'm junior and one of the first out, even with good tool skills.
do: Turn my resale side job into a real **online shop** with stock and repeat customers.
Ask about moving into a hands-on role like warehouse quality control.
feel: A jolt, **thrilled more than frozen**, with fear for the mortgage at night.
S2.quote: I'd tell my boss, you either make us the company that uses this, or we don't exist in two years.
fieldNote: Moves fast and runs **toward** the change, but still wakes up afraid of the mortgage.
Plans to leave early for a start-up rather than be last out.

steps.text: Build the phone resale into an online shop with real stock
Save six months of expenses and fix the mortgage rate
Apply to start-ups that need people who know AI tools
Pitch my boss on running Volt Trade's buying through AI

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say that's enough time to build something. At work I'd propose a pilot on automated reordering. Online I'd say learn the tools now and don't wait for a company to tell you.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I'm a little anxious but mostly motivated. Five years is enough to build a decent side business and a bit of savings, and I'd be 48 when AGI arrives, with Tolu's business still running. I'd be looking for something with real ownership, not another job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish an analytics course in the first year, then move toward a role that manages the AI system rather than buying by hand. My resale business would be pulling in maybe six hundred a month by year three. I'd keep paying the mortgage down faster and pick a second skill, like product sourcing from the supplier's side.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels like a green light with a time limit. I like that, it keeps me moving.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there any danger in having five years rather than two?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The danger is getting comfortable. Five years is long enough that you let it drift, and then year four arrives and you haven't done a thing. I'd write my milestones on the fridge for Tolu and the kids to see.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you teach Zainab about the next few years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd teach Zainab to be curious, ask good questions and not be scared. She already uses AI for homework, and I'd tell her to check its answers and ask why. And I'd say work is going to change a few times in her life, so learn how to learn.

say: I'd say five years is **enough time** to build something.
I'd propose a pilot on automated reordering at work.
think: I'm a little anxious but **mostly motivated**, and I'd be 48 when AGI arrives.
I want ownership, not another job.
do: Finish an **analytics** course in year one and move toward managing the AI system.
Grow resale income to about six hundred a month by year three.
feel: A **green light** with a time limit, which keeps me moving.
S3.quote: The danger is getting comfortable. Five years is long enough that you let it drift, and then year four arrives and you haven't done a thing.
fieldNote: Fears his own **drift** more than the technology, so he'd put milestones on the fridge.
Wants ownership instead of another job, and sees side income as the route.

steps.text: Finish an analytics course in the first year
Grow the phone resale business to six hundred a month
Move into a role managing the automated buying system
Write milestones on the fridge and track the mortgage balance

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say a decade is a gift, if people use it. At work I'd keep learning and keep sharing what I find. Online I'd say start something small, since a small business is the best way to learn.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I'd feel reasonably relaxed. By 2036 I'd be 53, the kids would be grown, and I'd probably have moved away from buying anyway. The risk is not AGI itself but wasting the ten years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep my day job, keep learning, and slowly build the resale shop into a proper business with a second person helping. I'd aim to pay the mortgage down well before then, and save for the kids' university. I'd do one big move, perhaps a degree in data or supply chain, part-time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels light and a bit exciting. There's a hum of unease, but mostly I'm looking forward to it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Ten years could be exciting or lazy. Which for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Exciting, but I know my habits, I'd get too comfortable at year six. So I'd have a yearly check-in with myself, what did I learn, what did I try, what do I stop. Tolu would keep me honest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want in place by 2030?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: By 2030 I'd want the mortgage cut by half, a business making real money, and a qualification in data. And the kids with a good attitude to learning. That's the plan, and it's enough.

say: I'd say a decade is a **gift**, if people use it.
I'd say start something small, since a small business teaches you most.
think: I'd feel **reasonably relaxed**; the risk is wasting the ten years, not AGI itself.
By 2036 I'd be 53 and probably moved away from buying anyway.
do: Grow the resale shop into a business with a **second person** helping.
Pay the mortgage down and save for the kids' university.
Study a part-time data or supply chain degree.
feel: Light and a bit **exciting**, with a hum of unease.
S4.quote: By 2030 I'd want the mortgage cut by half, a business making real money, and a qualification in data.
fieldNote: Treats ten years as a **project plan** with yearly check-ins and clear targets.
Knows his own tendency to get comfortable and builds guardrails against it.

steps.text: Hire a part-time helper for the resale shop within five years
Study a part-time data degree over several years
Cut the mortgage by half before 2030
Save for Zainab and Idris's university

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because I'd have a business that isn't big enough yet and a mortgage that doesn't wait. What would help is cheap business loans for people starting out, some paid time to retrain, and companies that tell their staff early what they plan to do.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask what I'd miss. I'd miss the guessing game of knowing what people will buy before they do, even when a machine does the sums. I'd like to find a way to keep playing it.

headlineQuote: I'd miss the guessing game of knowing what people will buy before they do, even when a machine does the sums.
portrait: Femi, 43, is a **junior buyer** of phone accessories at Volt Trade, with a salon-owner partner, two children and a mortgage.
He uses AI every day and already runs a side business reselling refurbished phones.
He worries about the firm's thin margins first and AI second, and runs toward change rather than waiting.
His mood moves from uneasy in mild worlds to alarmed when AGI is two years away, with action at each step.
biggestWorry: The **two-year** picture worries him most, because his business isn't big enough yet.
whatWouldHelp: Cheap **start-up loans**, paid retraining time, and employers who say early what they plan.
